articles.title: Bugs automated scanners miss that a human QA audit catches
articles.excerpt: Every website owner I know has run an automated scan at some point. The report comes back with a score, a list of missing alt attributes, a few performance warnings — and a general feeling that things…
articles.body: Every website owner I know has run an automated scan at some point. The report comes back with a score, a list of missing alt attributes, a few performance warnings — and a general feeling that things are probably fine. Scanners are genuinely good at what they check. The problem is what they can't check: anything stateful, anything visual in context, anything that requires actually completing a task like a customer. I've spent 10+ years as a QA engineer / SDET, and the bugs that cost businesses money are almost never in the scanner's report. They're in this list. 1. The form that says "sent" and sends nothing The contact form validates. The success message appears. The scanner sees a working form. What nobody checked: whether the message arrives.

articles.body: A vampire face that holds together while you stare at the screen may fall apart when you laugh, turn toward a friend, or lean back. But if your call shows your ordinary face, that points to a different problem. The browser experience in LiveFaceSwap AI is a live webcam preview. A working preview does not make that processed picture available as a camera in Zoom, Meet, or OBS. Browser testing lets you rehearse appearance and motion; verifying what another app receives is a separate task. The useful debugging question is: where does the picture first stop matching what you expect?

articles.title: Securing AI Coding Agents: Building Sandboxed, Policy-Driven Harnesses Against Prompt Injection, Log Poisoning, and Agent Drift
articles.excerpt: Originally published on tamiz.pro. AI coding agents are no longer experimental toys. They are autonomous systems that read your codebase, synthesize patches, execute shell commands, and push commits.…
articles.body: Originally published on tamiz.pro . AI coding agents are no longer experimental toys. They are autonomous systems that read your codebase, synthesize patches, execute shell commands, and push commits. The moment an agent can run npm install or git push , it stops being a chatbot and becomes a privileged process in your supply chain. The threat model shifts accordingly: prompt injection, log poisoning, and agent drift are no longer theoretical — they are the primary attack surface. This article dissects the architecture of a secure harness for AI coding agents. We'll walk through the threat model, then build a layered defense that combines OS-level sandboxing, policy-as-code enforcement, context separation, and deterministic replay.

articles.title: Stunning solar eclipse photos reveal giant hole and mysterious 'smoke rings' in the sun's atmosphere
articles.excerpt: Solar eclipse photography provides a unique vista into the processes taking place in the sun's upper atmosphere.
articles.body: Newly released photographs of the sun captured during the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse reveal the sun's outer atmosphere in unprecedented detail. The images, released by researchers working as part of the Solar Wind Sherpas project coordinated by the University of Hawaii, also show rare structures in the solar wind known as smoke rings. Named for their resemblance to the circles blown by smokers, these vortices were first identified in solar eclipse photographs captured in 2008. The researchers had long struggled to explain the processes behind their formation. They now know the rings are a result of the temperature differences in the coronal plasma and spread along the sun 's magnetic lines deep into interplanetary space.

articles.body: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.

articles.title: ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force . The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

articles.title: Meet Apeiron, Virgin Galactic's 1st 'Delta-class' space plane
articles.excerpt: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled its first "Delta-class" space plane, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.
articles.body: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name. Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents. The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.
